mainEntity.name: Should I contribute enough to get the full employer match?

acceptedAnswer.text: Generally yes — an employer match is effectively free money, and missing it is one of the most common ways people leave value on the table. The callout under your projected balance shows how much match you're capturing.

mainEntity.name: Does this account for contribution limits?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Your contributions are capped at the 2026 IRS limit for your age each year: $24,500 under 50, $32,500 from 50 (with the $8,000 catch-up) and $35,750 at ages 60–63.

mainEntity.name: What happens if I leave my job — can I keep my 401(k)?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — you can typically leave it with your former employer's plan, roll it into your new employer's plan, or roll it into an IRA, each with different pros and cons worth researching.

Traditional contributions reduce taxable income now with taxes owed on withdrawal; Roth contributions are taxed now but grow tax-free. The better choice often depends on whether you expect to be in a higher or lower tax bracket in retirement.

mainEntity.name: What happens to my employer match if I leave my job?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on your plan's vesting schedule — some employers require a certain number of years of service before you fully own matched contributions, so check your specific plan documents.

mainEntity.name: Is there a penalty for withdrawing from a 401(k) early?

acceptedAnswer.text: Withdrawals before age 59½ generally incur a 10% early withdrawal penalty on top of ordinary income tax, with some exceptions for specific circumstances — early withdrawal is generally discouraged given the impact on long-term growth.
